paraphrase: Thus spoke the arhat seer Maṅkhaliputta: one who stirs, trembles, is agitated, disturbed, moved, shaken and roused, and turns into this or that state, is not a protector (tāyin); one who does not stir or turn into this or that state is a protector — the protector saves himself and others from the four-bordered wilderness of saṃsāra. As the guide who knows the road leads others, the skilled physician frees the sick, and the one who knows the mixing of substances completes the work, so one who rightly knows the way of release and casts off attachment and aversion will reach perfection.
speaker: Maṅkhaliputta (as presented by the Jain text)
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ, which nonetheless calls him an arhat seer. Checked in the local GRETIL e-text; the chapter's first line is corrupt.

paraphrase: There are five kinds of 'ukkala': the staff-ukkala, who by the example of a staff (whose beginning, middle and end are only an aggregate) says 'there is no soul beyond the body' and cuts off rebirth; the rope-ukkala, who by the example of a rope teaches that there is only an aggregate of the five great elements and cuts off the continuity of saṃsāra; the thief-ukkala, who takes others' examples and arguments to promote his own side and cuts off compassion for others; the partial ukkala, who admits the soul but cuts it off in part by teaching its non-agency; and the total ukkala, who says nothing arises from anything and cuts off everything.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ. Checked in the local GRETIL e-text; the glosses of each ukkala are this unit's reading of a difficult passage (moderate).

paraphrase: The materialist's statement: 'Upward from the soles of the feet, downward from the tips of the hair, bounded by the skin — this is the self; this soul lives, this is its life. As burnt seeds do not sprout again, so when the body is burnt no body arises again. This alone is life; there is no other world, no fruit of good and bad deeds; souls are not reborn, merit and demerit do not touch them; good and evil are fruitless.'
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ. Checked in the local GRETIL e-text. The same skin-bounded formula opens the first man's view in Sūtrakṛtāṅga 2.1.

paraphrase: Forty-five seers — including Nārada, Asita Devala, Aṅgiras, Yājñavalkya, the Buddhist Vajjiyaputta, Mahākāśyapa and Śāriputra, Maṅkhali Gośāla, Pārśva and Vardhamāna — are each called 'arhat-ṛṣi' and give a short teaching on karma, passion, detachment and the path.
notes: Striking for honouring non-Jain seers as enlightened; list of names moderate confidence.
